counterexample: At any signal date d, the paper would hold mu~ and Sigma~ fixed at their one-time full-sample (Jan2000-Dec2015) EM estimate and re-estimate only Sigma_t on the trailing 52 weeks. The engine instead re-estimates mu~ and Sigma~ themselves at every signal date on an expanding window [start, d] (min 200 weeks). Concretely: at the first eligible signal (~nk=200, roughly 2003-11/12) the engine's mu~/Sigma~ come from only ~200 weeks of history, while a paper-faithful full-sample run at that same date would already be using jump parameters fitted on the complete 2000-2015 sample (including post-d weeks) - the two runs allocate differently at every single rebalancing date, not just early ones, since the engine's jump estimate keeps changing shape as the expanding window grows while the paper's is a single constant used throughout. This difference is disclosed, not hidden.
evidence: Section 4.3 ('Dynamics of out-of-sample ERC portfolios'): 'In the case of the ERC portfolio, it is common to consider a monthly rebalancing based on a one-year rolling covariance matrix' and 'we assume that the parameters pi, mu~ and Sigma~ are given once and for all, and are set to the previous estimates. At each rebalancing date, we have to estimate the covariance matrix Sigma_t for the normal regime.' Section 4.3's reported backtest uses the weekly mixture model (pi=0.5%, Table 9) with that monthly rebalancing + one-year rolling window - the same (frequency, rebalance) cell the engine implements (engine.R .N_WIN_NORMAL=52, .PI_JUMP=0.005, month-end signal grid .ME_OK).
